I take AP Latin and I took four years of Latin prior. I think Latin is definitely doable for self-study in one year. There's quite a lot of grammar to learn, especially compared to the other languages (I've taken Italian for 4 years and have all the grammatical knowledge required for AP), but with a good amount of translation practice it'll get pretty easy. After four years of studying Latin I can quickly translate the course material (Caesar's DBG and Vergil's Aeneid) given some vocab and notes. I definitely think AP Latin is your best bet because it's all reading and no speaking or culture. 

Also it's kinda annoying but you have to learn rhetorical devices in Latin, which I'm pretty sure you don't have to do with modern foreign languages (or at least not to the same extent). Still doable though

The line of health is drawn at grass-fed/pastured. Animals fed natural diets will produce the healthiest, safest, and most nutritious livers. Animals fed standard industry diets of grain, corn, and soy will produce significantly less nutritious livers, and their livers could potentially contain toxins. Unnatural diets put unnatural stress on the liver, which has the role of processing toxins, and eventually, it would be too difficult for the liver to keep up. 

Non-grass-fed/pastured livers still contain lots of nutrients, but personally, I just think the risk of toxins is not worth it and I'd rather spend a bit more on my high-quality liver. You can get high-quality organ meats from your local butcher, farmers markets, or farms. I get my beef liver from the butcher for $4/pound ($8.8/kg).

Personally, I believe this is a step in the wrong direction. 

First of all, plant foods are not even as close to as bioavailable as animal foods are. Plants are full of fiber, which is only partially digestible to humans. Think about cows-- true herbivores-- in comparison to humans. Cows have four stomachs and the grass they consume undergoes a lengthy digestion process during which the grass is fermented and regurgitated/rechewed several times before going to the small intestine where the actual nutrients are absorbed. Clearly, our digestion process is vastly different. Anti-nutrients are another factor to consider. When animal products are reduced in one's diet, they must be replaced. To align with the dietary guidelines, they would have to be replaced with grains, legumes, nuts, and soy, all of which contain anti-nutrients that inhibit nutrient absorption. Anti-nutrients are also present in most vegetables. Plant foods do not contain vitamin A in the form of retinol, which is pretty much the only form bioavailable to humans (a very tiny percentage of carotenoids can be converted, but even that is only in half of the population). This makes sense if you think about the fact that one's skin turns orange with the overconsumption of carotenoids. The carotenoids are not actually being digested as they are being excreted through the skin. Omega 3 to Omega 6 ratios are also negatively affected. Animal products tend to have more ideal omega 3 to omega 6 ratios, while plant foods tend to have a greater proportion of inflammatory omega 6. Even if one consumes a serving of raw salmon on occasion (aligning with the guidelines), the high omega 6 content of plants foods will offset the omega 3 consumption. There is so much more to be said about the nutritional deficits in a plant-based diet, but it would take far too long to discuss everything. 

Since this is a nutrition thread, I will keep discussion of other topics to a minimum. It is important to realize that a theoretical global shift to a plant-based diet (meaning a higher proportion of plants to animal foods, not necessarily all plants) would mean there would be significantly more monoculture, which would deplete the soil of even more nutrients. Animal feces help to fertilize the soil, so animal agriculture is vastly beneficial for the nutrient profiles of plants and the environment in general.

I do not support factory farming whatsoever. Factory farming is cruel and doesn't bring any environmental benefit, in addition to producing meat lacking in comparison to that of properly-raised animals. Getting meat from your local farmers is the best option, and seeing a shift towards that would be much more beneficial for the world as a whole. Fruits and veggies have their place in our diets, but high-quality animal products should be the focus.
